critique.good: Dish names and prices scan cleanly on one line. Ingredients and notes sit comfortably together, with most row heights driven by the longer ingredients; headers are clear and no words split.
critique.problems: Some notes have short, choppy lines, while the ingredient column still produces several five-line cells. The large empty areas under names and prices make the taller rows less compact to scan.
critique.cause: The 152px notes column has 131px of text space, while the 360px ingredient column has 339px. The descriptive text determines row height, leaving the compact first two columns mostly empty.

critique.good: The wider notes column gives notes natural, readable lines, and the identification and price columns remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: Ingredients wrap into long blocks, making every row taller and leaving substantial unused space below the shorter notes. This weakens the rhythm of the table and makes comparing dishes slower.
critique.cause: Reducing ingredients to 300px forces up to six lines, while the 212px notes column receives more space than its shorter content generally needs.

critique.good: Ingredients have generous line lengths, and dish names and prices remain intact.
critique.problems: Notes become narrow vertical stacks that dominate row height and are difficult to read. Large empty areas appear beneath the ingredients, so the extra ingredient width does not benefit the table as a whole.
critique.cause: The 92px notes column leaves only 71px for text; the 420px ingredient column takes space that notes need to wrap into sensible phrases.

critique.good: Dish names and prices stay on one line, headers are clear, and the descriptive columns are easy to distinguish. Notes generally fit within the height needed by ingredients.
critique.problems: The chicken ingredients end with the isolated word “sống.” on a fourth line. The special-dish note also occupies four short lines, giving it a rather ragged shape.
critique.cause: The 350px ingredient column falls just short of fitting the chicken description into three lines; the 162px note column wraps the special-dish note into four.

critique.good: The 370px ingredient column gives the chicken row a compact three-line description and produces the shortest table. Names, prices and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The notes are noticeably narrow and fragmented: the vegetarian note ends with a line containing only “10.000đ.”, while several notes occupy three or four short lines. This weakens the relationship between notes and their rows.
critique.cause: The 142px note column leaves only 121px for text, a consequence of assigning 370px to ingredients.

critique.good: The 172px note column gives the notes more natural line lengths, including a compact three-line special-dish note. Names, prices and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The chicken description again leaves “sống.” alone on its fourth line. Several ingredient cells have more frequent breaks than in r1B, without reducing the height of any row compared with r1A.
critique.cause: The 340px ingredient column trades away space from the longest and most consequential descriptions to widen notes.

critique.good: Dish names and prices scan cleanly on one line, and the generous ingredient column keeps descriptions readable. Notes fit within the height established by ingredients.
critique.problems: The first note ends with a short final line, while the last note spreads over four lines. The ingredient text is dense in the tallest rows.
critique.cause: The 152px notes column gives those phrases limited room; the 360px ingredient column must accommodate much longer descriptions.

critique.good: The widest ingredient column gives the main descriptions room, while names, prices and headers remain intact. Rows align clearly across the table.
critique.problems: The narrower notes column produces choppier phrasing, notably in the chicken note, without reducing any row height compared with r2A.
critique.cause: Moving 5px from notes to ingredients leaves notes at 147px, but 365px is not enough to remove an ingredient line in any row.

critique.good: The wider notes column improves some line breaks, including the chicken note, while all names, prices and headers remain intact. Row heights match the other designs.
critique.problems: The first ingredient description breaks the phrase “hành tím” across lines. The last note still occupies four lines, so the extra notes width has limited effect there.
critique.cause: Reducing ingredients to 355px changes its line breaks; 157px for notes is still too narrow to fit some longer phrases together.

understanding.purpose: Help diners choose a phở dish by comparing its price, ingredients and any accompanying notes.
understanding.reading: Readers scan dish names down the first column, compare prices, then read ingredients and notes across the chosen row. The long ingredient descriptions will largely determine row height, leaving room for notes to wrap alongside them.
groups: Món and Giá form the compact identification and price pair used for quick comparison.
Thành phần and Ghi chú are descriptive columns read alongside each dish; both can use multiple lines, but ingredients need more space.
keep_intact: Dish names and prices should fit on one line for easy scanning.
Individual words, currency amounts and identifiers should not be broken.
may_wrap: Ingredient descriptions can wrap naturally at spaces and punctuation.
Notes can wrap naturally, often within height already needed by the ingredients.

bad.why: The dish names and prices would wrap or split, while the narrow notes column would form a stack of short lines. The extra ingredient width does not compensate for making the menu harder to scan.

contrast.why: The dish names and prices would wrap or split, while the narrow notes column would form a stack of short lines. The extra ingredient width does not compensate for making the menu harder to scan.

final.rationale: r2A keeps dish names and prices on one line, so readers can scan the menu and compare prices quickly. Ingredients receive the largest measure, while notes retain enough width to read as phrases rather than a narrow stack. The rows remain distinct, and the chicken row avoids the isolated final word seen in some narrower ingredient columns.

general: Give identifying labels and values enough width to stay intact when they are important scanning anchors.
Allocate width according to content and reading role; judge line breaks and row rhythm as well as total height.
specific: This menu needs a much wider ingredient column than price column because the ingredients are long descriptions and the prices are short.
Around 355–365px for ingredients gives a useful balance with the notes in the rendered candidates.

final.tradeoffs: A wider notes column gives some notes more natural line breaks, while a wider ingredient column improves some ingredient lines. r3B favors ingredients but makes notes noticeably more fragmented; it remains readable.
final.uncertain: The ranges are approximate design tolerances, not verified breakpoints. They describe one column varying at a time with the others adjusted proportionally within the 719px limit; small changes can alter individual line breaks.

A.why: Dish names and prices stay on one line, while ingredients and notes both have comfortable widths. The rows remain easy to scan and compare.

B.why: The equal-width columns give excessive space to names and prices and leave ingredients in a narrow, heavily wrapped column. Tall rows contain large empty areas.

C.why: Ingredients and prices read well, but the narrow first column wraps most dish names across two or three lines, making the menu harder to scan.

D.why: Every price breaks across lines, and the narrow notes column produces very short lines and tall rows. The generous ingredient width comes at too high a cost to the other columns.

E.why: Names and prices stay intact and ingredients have ample room, but the relatively narrow notes column creates several short lines.

F.why: Names and prices stay intact, and ingredients and notes have a balanced share of space. The rows are compact without making either text column unduly narrow.

reviews.unsure: A gives notes more breathing room, while F gives ingredients more space; the preference between them depends on which text readers consult more often.

A.why: Dish names and prices stay on one line, and the broad ingredients column reads comfortably. Notes are somewhat narrow and wrap frequently.

B.why: Names and prices remain intact, with a useful balance between ingredients and notes. Some notes still wrap into short lines.

C.why: Equal column widths leave excessive space around names and prices while squeezing ingredients into long stacks of short lines, making rows difficult to scan.

D.why: Ingredients and notes have comfortable widths and prices stay intact, but most dish names wrap over two or three lines, weakening the row labels.

E.why: Prices break across lines and the narrow notes column produces fragmented text and tall rows, despite the ample ingredients column.

F.why: Dish names and prices stay intact, while ingredients and notes both have readable line lengths. The resulting rows have a clear, balanced rhythm.

reviews.unsure: A and B are close alternatives; the preferred balance between a wider ingredients column and fewer short lines in the notes is partly a judgment call.
